prompt: What is the third choice the lesson offers, besides patching the old system or rewriting it?

choices.text: Freeze the old system and build the new one beside it
choices.why: That is the rewrite with a freeze, and it still ends in one switch.

choices.text: Buy a product that replaces the old system
choices.why: Buying is lesson 8's subject; even a bought system would still need moving to.

choices.text: Replace it piece by piece while it runs
choices.why: Right: production runs on a mixture of old and new, and nobody picks a day to switch.

choices.text: Split the monolith into microservices in one programme
choices.why: A company-wide split is what the strategy postponed; the pattern moves one slice, not the whole.

prompt: Put the five moves of the strangler pattern in order.
hint: The first move makes every later one possible.
items: Put a facade in front of the old system
Build the new piece for one slice
Route that slice to the new piece, keeping the way back
Repeat until nothing is left on the old path
trap: Building the new piece before the facade leaves no way to send it a single slice, which turns the migration back into one big switch.

prompt: Why does the moving target from lesson 6 stop being a problem in a strangler migration?
hint: Where do changes to a moved event's holds get made?

choices.text: Other teams stop shipping until it ends
choices.why: Nobody at Coreto froze; the teams kept shipping throughout the twelve months.

choices.text: The facade translates old changes into new code
choices.why: The facade only routes; it never rewrites anybody's changes.

choices.text: Changes to moved slices are made on the new side
choices.why: Right: once a slice has moved, the old copy of it no longer changes, so there is nothing to chase.

choices.text: Twelve months is too short for the old code to change
choices.why: Eighteen months was enough for the rewrite's target to move; duration is not what solves it.

prompt: A team builds a complete new booking service beside the old one, and plans to send all traffic to it over one weekend, with a proxy in front. Is that a strangler migration, by the lesson?
hint: A facade is necessary; is it enough?

choices.text: No: it is a rewrite with one switch at the end
choices.why: Right: building it whole and switching at once brings back the rewrite's cutover risk, whatever sits in front.

choices.text: Yes, because a proxy in front is the facade
choices.why: The facade is the first move; the pattern is the slices that follow it, one at a time.

choices.text: Yes, provided the old service is deleted afterwards
choices.why: Deleting is the finish line, but this plan skips every step that makes the finish safe.

choices.text: No, because a strangler has to take at least twelve months
choices.why: Twelve months was Coreto's duration, not a rule; what matters is moving slice by slice.

prompt: Why did Coreto route seat holds by event rather than by a percentage of requests?
hint: Two requests for the same seat.

choices.text: Percentages are harder to configure in a proxy
choices.why: A percentage is the usual default and easy to set; the objection is what it does to one seat.

choices.text: Venues asked to be migrated one at a time
choices.why: No venue asked; the key was chosen by what must not be split.

choices.text: Events are easier to count on a progress chart
choices.why: The chart counts traffic, not events; counting was not the reason.

choices.text: One seat could be held in two stores at once
choices.why: Right: all holds for one event live on one side, so two buyers are never both told a seat is theirs.

prompt: What happens to the new service's answer during shadow traffic?
hint: The old code still answers the buyer.

choices.text: It is sent to the buyer whenever the old code fails
choices.why: A fallback would make the new code live; shadow answers reach no buyer.

choices.text: It replaces the old answer for small venues only
choices.why: Small venues went first for real routing; shadow is the step before routing anything.

choices.text: It is written to coreto-core's tables as a backup copy
choices.why: Shadow holds go to a separate store no buyer sees; writing them into live tables would corrupt real holds.

choices.text: It is recorded, compared, then thrown away
choices.why: Right: the comparison finds differences before any buyer meets them, as it did with the student half-price limit.

prompt: Why did Coreto reject the dual write, each confirmation written to both stores in the same request?
hint: One write succeeds and the other times out.

choices.text: Two stores, two answers, no owner
choices.why: Right: in the gap between two writes, a failure leaves two versions of who owns a seat and no owner to settle it.

choices.text: It doubles the database bill for the year
choices.why: The lesson's objection is correctness, not cost.

choices.text: Readers of the old tables would stop working
choices.why: Readers keep working either way; the chosen design also publishes into the old tables.

choices.text: Confirmations are too rare to be worth two writes
choices.why: Confirmations happen on every sale; frequency is not the problem.

prompt: Match each technique of the migration to what it buys.
hint: The table at the end of the section.

pairs.left: A seam inside the old system
pairs.right: One place to cut and to review
Holds for one event never split
Differences found before buyers meet them

pairs.left: One source of truth and a derived copy
pairs.right: Readers keep working while they migrate

right_distractors: A cutover on a single weekend

prompt: Another team strangles its e-mail notifications. Each message is independent of every other. By the lesson's reasoning, what routing key fits?
hint: Route by the thing that must not be split. Is there one?

choices.text: By event, as Coreto did, since it is the proven key
choices.why: Coreto chose events because a seat must not be split; notifications have no such unit.

choices.text: By customer, because customers complain individually
choices.why: Complaints do not decide the key; what must not be split does, and nothing here must.

choices.text: No key at all: shadow every message for the whole migration
choices.why: Shadow comes before switching; a migration that only shadows never moves anything.

choices.text: By percentage: nothing here must stay together
choices.why: Right: the percentage was wrong for seat holds only because two requests could touch one seat.

prompt: Coreto's new service reached 90% of reservation traffic at the end of month 8 and 100% at the end of month 12. How many months did the last 10% take?
Why did the last 10% of traffic take a third of the migration?
hint: Small in traffic, large in work.

choices.text: The big on-sales were saved for last
choices.why: Big on-sales moved once the load test passed, well before the tail; the tail was the rare paths.

choices.text: The new service slowed down under the extra load
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says the service struggled; the work was in the paths, not the capacity.

choices.text: Rare paths, each with its own work, several owned by other teams
choices.why: Right: hand holds at the door, school groups, festival passes and a partner contract each moved the chart by a point or two.

choices.text: The team was moved to other work after month 8
choices.why: That is the temptation the lesson warns about; Coreto finished the tail instead.

prompt: Why does the lesson call 90% the most expensive place to stop?
hint: Count the systems that would still be running.

choices.text: The last 10% carries the most valuable traffic
choices.why: The tail was the rare paths, not the valuable ones; the cost of stopping is in running two systems.

choices.text: Both systems run on, and the old debt's interest never reaches zero
choices.why: Right: facade, two stores, sync and old locks stay live, and anyone touching the old path still pays the tax.

choices.text: Venues are billed twice while two systems run
choices.why: Nothing reaches the venues' bills; the cost lands on Coreto's engineers.

choices.text: The routing table gets too large to maintain
choices.why: A table of events is small; the expense is everything the table keeps alive.

prompt: By the lesson, a strangler migration is finished on the day the old code is ___.
hint: Share of traffic is not the finish line.

prompt: A dashboard has shown "97% migrated" for six months, and the team behind it is now on another project. What would the lesson have them report and do?
hint: Two numbers, a list and a date.

choices.text: Call it done, since 97% is within any reasonable margin
choices.why: 97% means two systems still run; a migration is done when the old code is gone.

choices.text: Move the rest by percentage to finish faster
choices.why: The tail is not volume to shift; it is specific paths, each needing its own work.

choices.text: List what is left, with owners and a delete date
choices.why: Right: the second number only falls when something is deleted, and the tail moves once each path has an owner.

choices.text: Rewrite the remaining paths from scratch in one go
choices.why: That reintroduces the single cutover lesson 6 argued against, for the paths least understood.

prompt: Lesson 1 gave the Reservations team two quarters on the hold path. What percentage of reservation traffic did the new service carry at the end of month 6?
In what order did Coreto move events to the new service?

choices.text: Big on-sales first, since that is where the failures were
choices.why: That puts the riskiest move first, before the new service had proved anything.

choices.text: Small, then mid-size, then big after the load test
choices.why: Right: small mistakes first, and nothing reaches the on-sale path without load evidence, as lesson 1's policy says.

choices.text: Alphabetically by venue, so nobody felt left out
choices.why: The order was chosen by risk, not fairness between venues.

choices.text: The events whose holds were already expiring
choices.why: Holds expire in minutes for every event; it is why moving them is easy, not how the order was set.

prompt: Which of these are scaffolding, to be taken down when the migration finishes? Choose all that apply.
hint: What exists only because two systems run at once?

choices.text: The nightly reconciliation between the two stores
choices.why: Yes: with one store left there is nothing to reconcile.

choices.text: The path publishing confirmations into the old tables
choices.why: Yes: it exists for readers of the old tables, and they move before the end.

choices.text: The reservation service's own store of holds
choices.why: That is the new system, the thing the migration builds; it stays.

choices.text: The load test that replays an on-sale
choices.why: It is one of lesson 1's actions and keeps guarding the reservation path after the migration.

prompt: The Reservations team's first month shipped no new service, only one entry point inside the monolith. Why does the lesson say it paid for itself?
hint: Two things now had one place.

choices.text: One review point, and a place for the facade
choices.why: Right: it made lesson 1's review rule workable and gave the facade somewhere to sit.

choices.text: It removed the row locks from the hold path
choices.why: Nothing behind the entry point changed; the locks went with the new service.

choices.text: It cut the seat-hold interest to zero
choices.why: Interest only stops when the old code is gone; a seam alone leaves the locks in place.

choices.text: It let the partner integration read the new store
choices.why: The partner was in the tail and needed a conversation months later.

prompt: Halfway through the migration, the new service gets a group-booking rule wrong for one event. What does the strangler pattern let Coreto do that a rewrite would not?
hint: How was the event moved in the first place?

choices.text: Roll back the whole platform to last month's release
choices.why: Nothing that drastic is needed; the mistake is confined to one event.

choices.text: Change one row of the routing table and send that event back
choices.why: Right: the move was one row, so the way back is one row, before the event's next on-sale.

choices.text: Ship the fix straight to the old code instead
choices.why: The old code already handles group bookings; the fix belongs in the new service, with the event routed back meanwhile.

choices.text: Pause ticket sales until the rule is fixed
choices.why: Pausing sales is what the pattern exists to avoid; the old path is still there to serve the event.
